questions.q: Why is a Kubernetes Deployment manifest genuinely portable across AKS, EKS, and an on-prem cluster?
options: Because all three clouds run the identical physical hardware under the hood
Because the Kubernetes API is a conformant, versioned contract that every CNCF-conformant distribution implements identically
Because Kubernetes automatically rewrites the YAML to match whichever cloud it's deployed to
Because Deployments do not actually run containers, so there is nothing cloud-specific to vary
questions.explain: CNCF conformance testing guarantees that object kinds like Deployment behave identically across distributions, which is why the same manifest produces the same rolling-update and probe behavior everywhere.

questions.q: What actually happens when you apply a Service manifest with `type: LoadBalancer` to a cluster?
options: The cloud controller manager for that specific cluster provisions a cloud-specific load balancer, so the same YAML produces different real infrastructure on Azure vs. AWS vs. bare metal
Nothing — LoadBalancer is a deprecated field that modern Kubernetes ignores
Kubernetes core directly provisions a generic load balancer identical on every cloud
It silently converts itself into an Ingress resource
questions.explain: type: LoadBalancer is a real API field, but the behind-the-scenes provisioning is handled by a provider-specific cloud controller manager, so identical YAML produces an Azure Load Balancer, an AWS NLB/CLB, or nothing at all on bare metal without an add-on like MetalLB.

questions.q: Why can a PersistentVolumeClaim that works on AKS fail to bind on an EKS cluster using the identical manifest?
options: PersistentVolumeClaims are an AKS-only API object
EKS does not support persistent storage of any kind
AWS requires all storage requests to be made through the AWS CLI instead of Kubernetes manifests
StorageClass names are not standardized across clouds, so a referenced StorageClass like managed-csi may simply not exist on the EKS cluster
questions.explain: StorageClass names such as managed-csi (AKS) or gp3/ebs-sc (EKS) are cluster-specific; a PVC referencing a name that doesn't exist on the target cluster fails to bind even though the manifest itself is otherwise identical.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a Kubernetes-API field whose real-world behavior is provider-specific even though the field itself is generic?
options: The `replicas` field on a Deployment
The `selector.matchLabels` field on a Deployment
Ingress annotations, since different Ingress controllers (nginx vs. the AWS Load Balancer Controller) only honor their own annotation set
The `metadata.labels` field on a Pod template
questions.explain: Ingress is a standard API kind, but its annotations are interpreted by whichever controller is installed, so an nginx-specific annotation does nothing on a cluster running a different controller.

questions.q: What is the practical takeaway for treating Kubernetes workloads as portable?
options: Rewrite the entire manifest from scratch for every cloud instead of reusing any of it

Treat the core workload objects (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret) as the genuinely portable layer, and manage StorageClass names, Ingress annotations, and LoadBalancer behavior deliberately as an environment-specific overlay
Avoid Kubernetes entirely since nothing about it is actually portable
Assume every object in a manifest is fully portable and never review it per cluster
questions.explain: The lesson's core distinction is that the workload-definition layer travels unchanged, while storage, ingress, and load-balancer behavior are cloud-specific and need deliberate per-environment handling, often via overlays or per-cloud values files.
